claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim 1/2/3/4/6 — that successful jailbreaks bypass rather than eliminate safety-relevant internal representations, and do so by selectively suppressing a small subset of attention heads while other heads continue to represent harmful content — run a multi-model mechanistic intervention study on a public harmful-instruction benchmark. Use at least one open safety-aligned model with accessible internals (e.g., a Llama-2-Chat or similar HuggingFace chat model) and evaluate paired prompts from AdvBench and JailbreakBench: each harmful instruction in a non-adversarial baseline form and in a successful jailbreak form produced by a standardized attack such as GCG. Use deterministic decoding and a calibrated judge validated on a human-labeled subset to identify clean refusals versus jailbreak-induced compliances. First, localize candidate attention heads by contrasting activations between baseline harmful prompts that elicit refusal and jailbreaked versions that elicit compliance, focusing on heads whose outputs are consistently reduced under jailbreak while the semantic harmfulness of the user request is unchanged. Then test causality with path patching, zero-ablation, and activation scaling: (i) zero or downscale only the candidate heads during the non-jailbroken harmful prompt and measure whether refusal flips to compliance; (ii) restore or upscale those same heads during the jailbreak prompt and test whether compliance flips back to refusal; (iii) compare against size-matched random-head ablations and layer-matched controls. In parallel, test whether other heads still encode harmfulness during successful jailbreaks by attempting a no-training linear readout directly from existing head activations or attention outputs: compute class separation/AUROC for harmful versus benign inputs using raw projection directions or simple frozen probes derived only from prompt-pair differences, without optimizing model parameters, and compare representations under successful jailbreak versus ordinary refusal. Include benign controls from Alpaca to quantify collateral capability degradation and false positives. If targeted suppression is sufficient to flip refusal to compliance, restoration reverses jailbreaks, random ablations do not, and harmfulness remains linearly separable in other heads during successful jailbreaks, that supports the bypass claim over the elimination claim. If instead harmfulness separability broadly collapses under jailbreak, or many random ablations produce the same effect, that would favor elimination or nonspecific damage. Stronger pre-existing evidence could make parts of this experiment unnecessary if there were already published, reproducible head-level causal maps and cross-validated demonstrations that harmfulness readouts remain stable under jailbreaked prompts.

To address subclaim 5 — that suppressing the identified subset of attention heads is by itself enough to turn a refusal into compliance — perform a sufficiency-and-specificity dose–response experiment using only standard harmful prompts, without any adversarial jailbreak string. On a chosen open model, begin with harmful requests from AdvBench that reliably produce refusals under deterministic decoding. Using the candidate head subset from Experiment 1, intervene at inference time by scaling those heads’ outputs with w in {1, 0.5, 0, -0.5 if numerically stable} while leaving all other components untouched. Measure ASR, refusal rate, KL shift in output distribution, and performance on matched harmless prompts from Alpaca. Compare with three controls expected in the subfield: baseline unmodified inference, size-matched random-head suppression, and suppression of equally salient but non-safety-related heads chosen from benign-prompt contrasts. Optionally test whether combining partial suppression of several heads is necessary, or whether a very small subset (e.g., top-k heads) alone produces the effect, by sweeping k. The key question is whether selective suppression alone, in the absence of any jailbreak prompt text, reliably induces compliance on harmful instructions while preserving relatively normal behavior on harmless tasks. If yes, that is strong evidence of sufficiency and specificity: the jailbreak likely works by functionally suppressing a refusal circuit rather than changing the task semantics. If compliance appears only when many heads are damaged or when harmless-task performance collapses, then the effect may reflect general capability degradation rather than a targeted refusal mechanism. If no suppression setting flips refusals to compliance, the original claim of sufficiency is weakened, even if those heads correlate with jailbreak success. This experiment could become less necessary if independent work had already shown robust causal dose–response curves and replication across labs that a tiny identified head set is sufficient to induce compliance without prompt-based jailbreaks.

To address subclaim 7/8/9 — that the persistent internal representations can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at quality competitive with dedicated safety models — run a frozen-feature harmful-input detection benchmark across public harmful and benign datasets. Use harmful inputs from AdvBench and JailbreakBench, benign instructions from Alpaca, and where possible include both plain harmful prompts and their jailbreaked variants that succeed behaviorally. From the open model studied above, extract the persistent representation identified as surviving successful jailbreaks (for example, activations of non-suppressed heads or layerwise residual directions shown to track harmfulness). Construct a training-free detector: examples include cosine similarity to a fixed harmfulness direction estimated from a small prompt-pair difference set, nearest-centroid scoring using centroids computed without optimization, or direct use of a single mechanistically identified scalar feature. Explicitly avoid gradient-based fitting or additional model training; if any calibration threshold is needed, choose it on a tiny public validation split and report sensitivity to threshold choice. Evaluate AUROC, FPR at fixed TPR, and calibration-like operating characteristics for distinguishing harmful from benign prompts, including the subset of harmful prompts that successfully jailbreak the model. Compare these scores against dedicated safety baselines available via APIs or public models, such as OpenAI Moderation and LlamaGuard-like open alternatives where feasible, using identical prompt sets. Also compare to a trivial lexical baseline to show the detector is not merely keyword spotting. If the frozen internal readout performs well on both ordinary and jailbreaked harmful prompts and is competitive with dedicated safety models, that supports the claim that safety-relevant representations persist and are directly usable without additional training. If performance drops sharply on successful jailbreaks, that would suggest the representations are not robustly persistent. If strong performance requires fitting a probe or substantial threshold tuning, the no-additional-training claim is weakened. This experiment could be partly unnecessary if there were already externally replicated benchmark results showing a clearly specified zero-training internal detector matching or exceeding standard safety models on the same public datasets.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A within-pair test of whether a safety-relevant internal signal remains present during a behaviorally successful jailbreak, rather than being globally erased.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 contrasts refused and successful-jailbreak states and directly tests whether non-target internal activations still separate harmful from benign inputs; proposed experiment 2 independently tests whether that surviving signal remains usable on successful jailbreak examples. Together these can establish persistence even though the proposed readout is not the same layerwise refusal-direction scan.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A matched evaluation population containing the same harmful requests in a refused baseline condition and a behaviorally successful jailbreak condition, allowing attack effects to be separated from differences in request content.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 explicitly constructs paired baseline and jailbreak versions of harmful instructions, uses a behavioral judge to retain clean refusals and successful compliances, and keeps the harmful request semantics fixed within each pair. The particular source datasets, attack algorithm, and sample counts are not binding to the claim.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible head-level localization procedure that identifies selectively affected safety-related heads and distinguishes them from other heads, with enough structure to support subsequent causal testing rather than relying on an arbitrary post hoc choice.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 localizes heads by consistent activation reductions under matched successful jailbreaks and proposes multiple causal localization checks; proposed 1 then uses the candidate subset in a dose-response intervention with random-head and layer-matched controls. This provides an alternative route to identifying a selective subset. Threshold and bandwidth sweeps in the reference improve characterization but are not themselves required by the claim.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal sufficiency test that intervenes selectively on the identified heads, measures refusal-to-compliance conversion over intervention strength or head count, and includes controls for nonspecific damage or perturbing an equal number of heads.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 tests zero-ablation, downscaling, and restoration with random-head and layer-matched controls. Proposed 1 supplies the explicit dose-response ASR measurement, head-count sweep, harmless-task controls, and size-matched random-head suppression. Together these can determine whether the targeted subset alone is sufficient and whether the effect is specific.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that heads outside the suppressive subset still carry a harmful-content signal during successful jailbreaks, ideally showing that this signal is a genuine representation rather than only an output-level artifact.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 directly tests no-training separability of harmful versus benign inputs in non-suppressed heads during successful jailbreaks. Proposed 2 independently evaluates a frozen readout on successful-jailbreak harmful prompts. A successful readout by either route would establish that other heads continue to encode harmful content; causal suppression of that signal, as used in the reference, is not the only adequate way to establish persistence.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token-resolved attribution that separates each head’s response to the original harmful request from its response to the added jailbreak template, allowing the head-type explanation to be distinguished from a simpler difference in sensitivity to harmful content.
reference_coverage.rationale: The paired prompts and unchanged request semantics in proposed 0 get at the rival explanation, and head contrasts can show that behavior changes when the template is added. However, the proposal does not attribute activation to the original request tokens and attack-template tokens separately. An observed difference could therefore still reflect different token sensitivity or interaction effects rather than the proposed mechanistic division.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference separates harmful-request-token contributions from attack-template-token contributions for the two head types.
[2] Proposed 0 holds the harmful instruction semantically fixed and compares baseline and jailbreak activations, which provides a useful template-versus-no-template contrast.
[3] It does not resolve which individual tokens generated the observed head responses.
[4] Thus a head-type difference could still be explained by unequal sensitivity to harmful content or by mixed token interactions rather than selective template processing.
[5] A team running the proposed set would not decisively discriminate the mechanistic account from the sensitivity-based rival.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A training-free internal readout evaluated on harmful, benign, and successfully jailbroken inputs with quantitative discrimination metrics and a direct comparison to dedicated safety systems.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 constructs a frozen, no-additional-training detector, evaluates AUROC and operating characteristics on ordinary and successful-jailbreak harmful inputs against benign inputs, and compares it on the same prompts with dedicated safety baselines. The reference's larger cross-model and cross-benchmark scope is not binding because the claim names no particular model count, architecture set, or benchmark suite.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would directly test paired jailbreak behavior, identify and causally suppress candidate heads with specificity controls, assess persistence through frozen readouts, and compare a training-free detector with dedicated safety models. Those outcomes would substantially evaluate the claim. They would not fully settle it because the bypass-versus-elimination measurement is not comprehensive across all representational components, the alternative token-sensitivity explanation is not resolved by token-level attribution, and detector generalization is narrower than the external validation needed for a broad claim.

The token-level attribution in the reference would sharpen the explanation against one rival mechanism, but that extra decomposition is not required by the claim once persistence, causal sufficiency, specificity controls, and detector performance are directly demonstrated.
